title: Wireless Electronic Inclinometers Versus the Pendulum in the Inclining Test: A Field Evaluation on Two Fishing Vessels
content: The inclining test determines a ship's metacentric height (GM) from the heel produced by shifting known weights. The pendulum remains the reference instrument, but it is read by eye and exposed to parallax, reading and transcription errors. This study compares a conventional pendulum with four low-cost wireless inclinometers (WitMotion WT9011DCL), logged in real time by a mobile application (EstabApp), in two inclining tests of fishing vessels in Peru. Linearity, each instrument's own precision (Grubbs' method, which needs no reference value), step-by-step agreement (Bland–Altman) and the effect on GM were evaluated with the pendulum data as recorded. The sensors' own random error was 0.004–0.015°, against 0.013 and 0.041° for the pendulum, and 77–95 % of the residual scatter was common to all instruments, i.e. it originated in the test rather than in the angle measurement. The sensor-mean GM differed from the pendulum GM by 3.9 and 8.4 mm (0.37 and 0.76 %), without statistical significance. On vessel B, the larger pendulum error came from one physically inconsistent reading, recorded as such on the field sheet and undetectable by the standard procedure. Under real test conditions the sensors were thus more precise than the pendulum, while removing human reading errors and enabling real-time supervision. Replacing two of the three pendulums recommended by the 2008 IS Code with such sensors is justified; full replacement should be assessed by the authorities under a dedicated validation protocol.
